articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress on Monday said Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union minister Amit Shah must sack Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar if they are genuinely concerned about Delhi's traders and want to stop the INDIA bloc's November 1 rally at Ramlila Maidan.In a post on X, Congress MP Pawan Khera said the government's refusal to remove CEC Gyanesh Kumar was the real issue, not the protests."If Modi and Shah are truly concerned about Delhi’s traders and genuinely want to stop the 1st November rally, they must sack Gyanesh Gupta and address our demands immediately. The ball is in their court," Khera said."Protests, rallies and demonstrations demanding an end to ECI-administered Vote Chori and election rigging for the RSS-BJP are acts of patriotism. The protests are not the problem. The problem is the government’s obstinacy to save the chair of a bureaucrat who wins elections for them. Delhi’s traders, too, must fulfil their patriotic duty by demanding that the government remove Gyanesh Babu," he added.This comes after Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi expressed solidarity with Delhi's traders and accused the government of disrupting business by shutting metro services, sealing roads and locking down the capital."To every trader in Delhi: We love you and hear you. The Govt shut the metro, sealed our roads and locked down our capital. With a stolen vote nothing is safe - your shop, your savings, your children’s future. Tell Modi to sack accused no. 4, Gyanesh Kumar and the protests will stop in 30 seconds," Rahul said.Earlier on Saturday, traders had urged Rahul and the Congress to call off their protests, citing business losses as they were forced to shut their establishments amid demonstrations.The Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI) also urged Rahul to postpone the INDIA bloc's November 1 rally at Ramlila Maidan, warning that the demonstration could disrupt business worth Rs 10,000 crore during the peak Diwali shopping season."This year, Dhanteras falls on Friday, November 6, Diwali on November 8 and Bhai Dooj on November 10. People begin shopping for Dhanteras and Diwali a week in advance. In Delhi alone, Dhanteras-related business across sectors such as gold and silver, utensils, electronics, textiles, dry fruits, sweets, automobiles, vehicles, property and gift items amounts to approximately Rs 25,000 crore. This trade is the backbone of Delhi's economy," the letter read.The traders' body said markets typically see a surge in activity about a week before festivals, raising concerns over the timing of the rally. CTI president Goyal added that traders in Delhi had already suffered losses of around Rs 3,000 crore in October due to rallies, marches and road closures in Connaught Place, India Gate and central Delhi.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: The ‘My Fair Lady’ and ‘Camelot’ copyrights help fund music education through the Frederick Loewe Foundation’s grants of up to $800,000 a year
articles.summary: The copyrights behind Broadway musicals such as My Fair Lady and Camelot form part of the legacy of composer Frederick Loewe; the work continues to be
articles.body: The copyrights behind Broadway musicals such as My Fair Lady and Camelot form part of the legacy of composer Frederick Loewe; the work continues to be managed by the Frederick Loewe Foundation. Established in 1956, the New York non-profit organisation holds the copyrights Loewe bequeathed to it after he died in 1988. According to its official website, the foundation makes grants of up to $800,000 a year to preserve the composer’s musical legacy, raise awareness of his work, support music education and encourage musical theatre.How do the “My Fair Lady” and “Camelot” copyrights help fund music educationThe composer established the Frederick Loewe Foundation in 1956 as a New York non-profit corporation. Its original purpose was to make charitable contributions to causes of his choice. After Loewe died in 1988, he bequeathed ownership of his copyrights to the foundation, giving the organisation control over the rights to his musical compositions and his interests in works he created with Lerner.The foundation states that its present-day activities include protecting Loewe’s musical legacy, increasing public awareness of his work, supporting music education and encouraging musical theatre. The board of directors determines the direction of its grants. This places the preservation of the composer’s work alongside the organisation’s charitable objectives, which include helping to sustain music education and the wider appreciation of musical theatre.How much does the Frederick Loewe Foundation award in grants annuallyThe foundation states that it makes grants of up to $800,000 annually. The grants are intended to “protect and preserve Frederick Loewe's musical legacy and expand public awareness of the composer and his music as well as to support music education and to encourage musical theatre”.The annual grant figure represents the maximum amount, rather than a guarantee that the full sum will be distributed every year. The organisation’s grant-making priorities are determined by its board of directors. Its published information therefore establishes both the scale of funding it can provide and the purposes for which the grants are intended, without specifying that every grant is funded by an individual musical or copyright payment.Who can apply for grants from the Frederick Loewe FoundationThe foundation publishes information about its grant application process on its Grants page. It states that proposals should be no longer than two pages and that applicants should submit them by email. The organisation adds that it will contact applicants if it requires further information. Its grant guidance also specifies that, as a tax-exempt organisation under Section 501 of the US Internal Revenue Code, it can make grants only to other qualified tax-exempt organisations.The foundation’s licensing activities and charitable grant-making are distinct parts of its work. It manages Loewe’s copyrights and works with Lerner’s heirs on the licensing of their shared musical properties, while its grants support the objectives established by its board. Through these activities, the organisation continues to preserve the composer’s legacy while supporting music education and musical theatre, in keeping with the purposes described on its official website.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1969, Jack Klingbeil and his wife started a miniature railway for their children in Alaska; by 2026, it had grown into a public family attraction with 3.5 miles of track, bridges and tunnels across 18 acres
articles.summary: A miniature railway that Jack Klingbeil and his wife built for their children in 1969 now carries visitors along 3.5 miles of track in Wasilla, Alaska.
articles.body: A miniature railway that Jack Klingbeil and his wife built for their children in 1969 now carries visitors along 3.5 miles of track in Wasilla, Alaska. The line winds through tunnels, over bridges and past scale-model towns on 18 acres of woodland, according to a report by Dave Allgood for Aging Untold, published on 9 July 2026 and carried by Atlanta News First. The railway runs at one-eighth scale. Klingbeil said the reason for starting it was simple. “My wife and I founded this back in 1969 so our children could have something to do and stay out of trouble,” Klingbeil said.A family business across generationsThe railway is still run by the family, Aging Untold reported. Klingbeil’s daughter checks in passengers, and his grandson helps run the trains. Visitors ride or straddle the miniature cars as they pass through wooded terrain, with stops along the route for photographs. The trains weigh about 1,000 pounds each and can carry up to 10 passengers on a run, the report said. Some can haul larger groups. One visitor told Aging Untold that the family first came on Mother’s Day about two years earlier and had returned for another ride.From Anchorage to WasillaKlingbeil began the railway in Anchorage in 1969, according to an earlier report by Allgood for Alaska’s News Source, published in June 2024. The line later moved to the Palmer Fairgrounds and then to Wasilla, where it had stood for the previous 14 years at the time of that report. The report did not say why the railway moved. Alaska’s News Source marked the railway’s 55th year in that 2024 piece. The railway operates as the Alaska Live Steamers Railroad Museum and the Alaska Central Railroad. Its engines are built on site, and the only item the group buys is the track itself. A full tour lasts 55 minutes. It crosses trusses, bridges and ponds and passes through a series of model villages. Allgood described the attention to detail as an engineering feat. He also wrote that the ride took him back to childhood, when the woods felt like a magical place.Run by volunteersAlaska Live Steamers is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit dedicated to preserving and teaching railroad history, according to notes published with the Alaska’s News Source report. The organisation says it is run only by volunteers and that nobody is paid for their time. The notes explain where the income goes. “All the money we make from train rides and donations is used to maintain the facility and extend the track.” Those who wish to donate or volunteer can contact the Alaska Central Railroad through its Facebook page or at alaskasteamers.com.Track gauge, past plans and accessA 2014 account on the Alaska Rails site, written by railfan John Combs, described the line as a 7½-inch gauge railway and called Klingbeil the patriarch of Alaska Live Steamers. Combs wrote that Klingbeil had put his heart and soul into it, with the help of dedicated volunteers. At that time, the group planned to let visiting live steamers run their own equipment on the track and use sidings leading to private overnight cabins. This report could not confirm whether the cabins have since been built. The railway also has a carriage for passengers with special needs, according to the organisation’s notes. “Everyone can ride the train. We even have a chair car for those with special needs!” The group asks visitors to tell it in advance if the chair car is required.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia turns to Maven-like AI system to hunt Houthi missiles; why it may not be effective
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia is turning to artificial intelligence to sharpen its battlefield edge against Yemen’s battle-hardened Houthis, betting that US-backed
articles.body: Saudi Arabia is turning to artificial intelligence to sharpen its battlefield edge against Yemen’s battle-hardened Houthis, betting that US-backed targeting technology can help it track mobile missile launchers, detect drone threats and strike faster.But as the kingdom seeks a technological advantage against a group that has withstood years of military pressure, a critical question remains: can AI change the course of a war that advanced weapons alone have failed to win?According to CNN report that quoted unnamed US officials, American personnel are helping Saudi military officers use an AI-assisted battlefield targeting tool similar to the US military’s Maven Smart System.The support includes intelligence and targeting assistance, with between 100 and 200 US troops reportedly deployed as part of a joint force command.The move comes as Saudi Arabia faces persistent security threats from Yemen’s Houthi movement, which has used drones and ballistic missiles to target military installations and critical infrastructure.Despite years of military operations, the group has retained the ability to launch attacks, highlighting the challenge of tracking mobile weapons and identifying targets before they can be moved or concealed.What is Maven AI and how can it help Saudi Arabia?At the centre of the reported effort is the US military’s Maven Smart System (MSS), an artificial intelligence platform developed under Project Maven, launched by the Pentagon in 2017.The system uses AI to analyse intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance data, including satellite imagery and drone footage, helping military personnel identify potential targets and assess battlefield activity more quickly.Unlike traditional intelligence analysis, which often requires personnel to manually review hours of surveillance footage, Maven can process large volumes of data, identify patterns and flag potential military targets such as vehicles, missile launchers and other equipment.For Saudi Arabia, the technology could help track Houthi missile launchers, detect drone activity and identify threats to military bases, airports and oil infrastructure.By reducing the time between detecting a potential target and deciding how to respond, AI-assisted systems could give Saudi forces a better chance of acting before mobile weapons are relocated or concealed.It brings information from multiple sources into a shared interface, helping commanders build a clearer picture of the battlefield and make decisions faster.The system could also improve coordination between intelligence analysts and military commanders by combining surveillance feeds and threat assessments in one place.This could help Saudi forces prioritise emerging threats, allocate surveillance resources and coordinate responses more efficiently, particularly when facing multiple drone and missile threats in quick succession.Why Maven AI may struggle against the HouthisDespite its ability to accelerate target detection, the US military’s Maven Smart System faces significant challenges in Yemen, where Houthi forces use mobile, truck-mounted ballistic missiles and small drone swarms while operating from hills, canyons and rugged terrain.According to Deutsche Welle (DW) report, these tactics could allow Houthi fighters to relocate before an AI-assisted system can help commanders identify and authorise a strike. Dust storms, changing terrain, dense foliage and deliberately planted decoys can further reduce the system’s effectiveness.The technology also raises concerns over targeting errors and civilian casualties. Deutsche Welle (DW) reported that a US missile strike on a school in Iran, which killed nearly 200 people, mostly children, was among the targets associated with the US military’s AI-assisted targeting operations.The incident underscores the risks of relying on flawed intelligence or inadequate human verification, although it does not establish that AI alone caused the strike.The broader challenge is strategic rather than purely technological. Antony Loewenstein, an independent journalist who has researched AI-assisted military technology, told DW that he did not believe such tools would make a significant difference in defeating the Houthis, warning of the risk of large-scale civilian casualties.The group’s ability to withstand destruction means faster targeting may improve Saudi Arabia’s operational efficiency without delivering a decisive military victory.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Who checks the power?' Ex-SC judge calls for safeguards in poll panel appointments
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former Supreme Court judge Abhay Oka has called for a legal framework to ensure that the appointment of election commissioners remains free
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Supreme Court judge Abhay Oka has called for a legal framework to ensure that the appointment of election commissioners remains free from political dominance. He stressed that independent institutions are essential to protecting democracy.Speaking at a lecture titled "Freedom of Speech and Us" in Thane on Sunday, Justice Oka (retd) questioned the safeguards in place to ensure accountability in constitutional appointments and called for a more independent selection process.Oka cited a proposal by former deputy prime minister Lal Krishna Advani for a collegium system to appoint election commissioners. "Former Deputy Prime Minister Lal Krishna Advani had proposed a collegium system nearly 14 years ago, which would have included the Prime Minister, Law Minister, Leaders of the Opposition in both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, and the Chief Justice of India, to ensure a truly independent selection process," he claimed.He also questioned what would happen if an election commissioner, such as Gyanesh Kumar, were removed from office, highlighting the need for clear legal provisions governing such appointments and ensuring institutional independence.Reiterating the importance of free and fair elections, Oka said freedom of speech was equally vital to democracy. Every citizen must be able to express their views and perspectives, he said, adding that disagreements should be addressed through debate rather than violence."To preserve our nation's democracy, freedom of speech must be protected, as life loses its meaningful essence without it," he added.The former judge also criticised what he described as "systematic environmental exploitation", linking rising temperatures in Thane and Mumbai to the loss of green cover."Temperatures in Thane and Mumbai touching 38 to 40 degrees Celsius were unprecedented. Thousands of trees had been cut down across Thane over the past decade to clear space for various projects, the consequences of which citizens are now bearing," he said.Oka lamented the lack of environmental sensitivity among political leaders. He said maintaining a scientific temper did not mean opposing religion, citing idol immersion in natural water bodies as an example of practices that conflict with scientific stewardship.He also questioned the proposed circular metro project in Thane, arguing that citizens had the right to scrutinise large public spending decisions. He asked whether the ₹12,000 crore earmarked for metro corridors could be put to better use through alternatives such as road optimisation and a significant expansion of the Thane Municipal Transport fleet.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In September 2026, Halle Berry joined a jury choosing five emerging women filmmakers for Tribeca and Chanel's programme; the winner received $120,000 to make a short film, while four others earned $10,000 grants
articles.summary: Oscar-winning actor Halle Berry joined a panel of well-known film industry figures in September 2026 to choose five emerging women and non-binary
articles.body: Oscar-winning actor Halle Berry joined a panel of well-known film industry figures in September 2026 to choose five emerging women and non-binary filmmakers for a special mentorship programme in New York City. The three-day programme offered expert guidance and a production grant to help bring a short film to life. The initiative, called Through Her Lens: The Tribeca CHANEL Women's Filmmaker Program, marked its 11th year by pairing five selected creative teams with experienced writers, directors and producers. Organized by Tribeca Enterprises and luxury brand Chanel, the programme offers creative advice and professional guidance on script development, pitching, directing and production planning. According to 10 Magazine USA, writer-director Gem Little and producer Kseniya Yorsh won the top prize for their proposed short film, COWARDS. The winning team received a $120,000 grant and production support from Tribeca Studios to fully fund and make the film. The other four finalist teams each received a $10,000 grant to help develop their projects further.High-profile jury selects winning narrativeAt the end of the workshop, a selected panel of actors, directors and cinematographers reviewed the five projects and chose a winner. Halle Berry was joined on the jury by actors Meg Ryan, Regina King and Ella Rubin, along with cinematographer Autumn Durald Arkapaw. The winning film, COWARDS, follows an eleven-year-old girl named Diamond as she deals with difficult family relationships during a single summer day in Chicago. The story is based on writer-director Gem Little's own experiences of living with different relatives while her mother was in prison.In a formal statement published by 10 Magazine USA, the jury said the project "touched us the most as a compassionate, strong example of a story that is needed in our country right now." The selected teams also received direct guidance from experienced film professionals who served as mentors during the workshop. The 2026 mentors included director Celine Song, playwright Aleshea Harris, producer Ellen Goldsmith-Vein, actor Fala Chen and director Gina Prince-Bythewood.Three days of intensive industry instructionThe official programme overview on the Tribeca website explains that the three-day autumn workshop helps filmmakers improve their scripts, develop a clear creative vision and learn how to present their projects to potential investors. After an open application process, a selection committee chooses five projects with completed scripts that are ready for production. Applicants must submit a finished screenplay and show at least one project they have directed before. During the workshop, the teams take part in one-on-one advice sessions, group discussions and meetings with other filmmakers. The programme covers practical parts of independent filmmaking, including choosing key creative staff, working within a budget and finding opportunities at international film festivals. The initiative aims to reduce long-standing gender gaps in filmmaking by giving emerging directors financial support and valuable industry contacts. According to Tribeca, the winning team continues to receive guidance after filming ends and the completed short film moves into distribution. Speaking about the effect of the workshop, director Gem Little told 10 Magazine USA that "this experience changed me." She highlighted the supportive atmosphere created by the mentors and other participants.Sustained support for independent storytellingSince it began, the partnership between Tribeca and Chanel has aimed to help women and non-binary writers and directors move their projects from early script development to a commercial release. Previous editions of the programme have offered advice from directors Kathryn Bigelow, Patty Jenkins, Karyn Kusama and Olivia Wilde. Actors Glenn Close, Courteney Cox, Sarah Jessica Parker and Lucy Liu have also taken part. The grant awarded to Little and Yorsh will cover the full production of COWARDS. Tribeca Studios will also provide practical support through post-production. Meanwhile, the four other teams will each receive $10,000 to continue developing their projects and move closer to making their films. With the 2026 programme now complete, the organizers confirmed that applications for the next edition will reopen ahead of the 2027 Tribeca Festival. The festival is scheduled to take place in New York from June 3 to June 12.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Algeria’s president orders troop deployment to neighbouring Niger
articles.summary: Niger requested troops to secure shared energy interests in what would be Algeria’s first deployment abroad since 1973.
articles.body:
Algeria’s President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has ordered troops to neighbouring Niger to protect energy and economic interests shared by both countries.

The decision, announced by Algeria’s presidency on Monday, came after both chambers of parliament approved the deployment in an emergency session on Sunday.

The presidency said authorities in Niger had requested military assistance.

If carried out, it would be Algeria’s first overseas military deployment since 1973, when it sent soldiers to support Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war.

The move marks a departure from Algeria’s longstanding reluctance to intervene militarily beyond its borders.

A 2020 constitutional reform allows the president to authorise overseas deployments with the approval of at least two-thirds of legislators in each parliamentary chamber.

Algeria sent fighter jets and support aircraft to Niger in August after what Algerian officials described as an attempt to destabilise its military government.

The presidency said the deployment decision was made under provisions of Algeria’s constitution allowing the military to operate abroad with parliamentary approval.

It has not been announced how many soldiers will be sent or when.

Algerian Senator Belkacem Boulghiti told reporters after Sunday’s parliamentary vote that the soldiers would protect economic infrastructure, particularly Algerian oil facilities in Niger.

He said Algeria was “not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger”, describing the mission as a response to changing security conditions in the Sahel region.

Algeria’s state-owned energy company, Sonatrach, has been working with Niger on the proposed Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline. It would carry natural gas from Nigeria through Niger to Algeria for export to European markets.

Niger and neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso have faced years of attacks by armed groups linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS).

All three countries are governed by military leaders who seized power in coups and subsequently formed the Alliance of Sahel States, a regional political and security bloc.

The deployment follows an improvement in relations between Algeria and Niger, which has been led by General Abdourahamane Tiani since a 2023 military coup that Algeria initially condemned.

Tensions deepened in April last year after Algerian forces shot down a Malian drone near the border, prompting the three alliance members to recall their ambassadors from Algiers.

articles.title: How Venezuela’s earthquake amputees adapt to life without limbs
articles.summary: Experts say recovery for earthquake survivors will likely be a lifelong endeavour, given the physical and mental toll.
articles.body:
Ricardo Contreras’s new leg rests on a wooden countertop.

More than four months after twin earthquakes struck Venezuela, the 24-year-old is still recovering from his injuries.

When he was trapped beneath the rubble on the night of June 24, he waited hours to be rescued. His left leg had been pinned beneath a fallen door frame, limiting its blood circulation. It had to be amputated.

“One of the biggest achievements is that we survived,” Ricardo said, glancing towards his 16-year-old brother, Andres Contreras. “At first, when I found out Andres was well, I didn’t care about my leg too much. I would have chosen a thousand times over for Andres to be OK.”

But now Ricardo is adapting to his new reality.

He and his brother are still undergoing physiotherapy for their injuries. On a scorching afternoon, he sits in a small workshop in the hills of northwestern Caracas, waiting to do rehabilitation exercises to prepare for his new prosthetic leg.

“Now it’s about regaining a little of the independence I had before the earthquake, because that’s what limits me most," Ricardo said.

But recovery is only part of the challenge he is facing. His parents died in the collapse.

Resources and aid have also grown scarcer, particularly as global attention faded and international donations dried up.

As of September, the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) said it had secured only $29.5m of the $65.7m needed to continue its earthquake support in Venezuela, a shortfall of 55 percent.

Separately, that same month, the International Red Cross said its Venezuela response effort was only 39.8 percent funded.

Not only are survivors like Contreras left to grapple with loss of limbs and family members, but they now face the prospect of lifelong health costs — with dwindling support.

articles.title: A Kentucky church bought residential land for a Virgin Mary shrine, but neighbours challenged the plan; now the US Supreme Court has agreed to hear the zoning dispute
articles.summary: A proposed shrine to the Virgin Mary has brought a Kentucky church group into a dispute over residential zoning, with the case now heading to the highest
articles.body: A proposed shrine to the Virgin Mary has brought a Kentucky church group into a dispute over residential zoning, with the case now heading to the highest court in the United States. The Missionaries of Saint John the Baptist, a nonprofit formed by Roman Catholic priests, wants to build the religious structure on a neighbouring plot it purchased for that purpose. Residents challenged the plan, raising concerns about the effect on their neighbourhood and whether local zoning rules had been properly applied. As reported by the Associated Press (AP), after the dispute moved through Kentucky’s courts, the US Supreme Court agreed on October 1, 2026, to consider the case, bringing a local planning disagreement into a wider legal debate over religious freedom and land use.Kentucky church shrine plan faces residential zoning restrictionsThe Missionaries of Saint John the Baptist acquired a residential property in Park Hills, Kentucky, a suburb of Cincinnati, intending to use it for a shrine dedicated to the Virgin Mary. The group maintains that the project forms part of its religious mission and that federal law provides grounds for challenging restrictions that prevent it from going ahead.The dispute centres on how far religious organisations can rely on federal protections when local planning rules limit the use of land for religious purposes. The group has argued that the relevant law can prevent government authorities from enforcing land-use regulations that place a substantial burden on religious exercise in certain circumstances.Neighbours challenge Kentucky church shrine plan over zoning rulesThe proposal faced opposition from a family living in the neighbourhood. Reportedly, the family raised concerns about traffic and argued that the shrine could add to existing problems in the area. It challenged the local zoning board's decision in state court, ultimately securing a ruling against the church group's plans.The case turned in part on whether the zoning board had the legal authority to grant a variance allowing the religious structure to be built on the residential tract. In December 2025, the Kentucky Supreme Court concluded that the board lacked that authority.The ruling left the Missionaries of Saint John the Baptist unable to rely on the variance to move forward with the project. The organisation subsequently sought review by the US Supreme Court, arguing that the state court had interpreted federal protections for religious land use incorrectly. The opposing family has maintained that the church group knew the property was covered by zoning restrictions that prevented the proposed use when it bought the land. It has also questioned why the shrine could not be constructed on property already belonging to the church rather than on a neighbouring residential plot.Religious land use law at the centre of Kentucky shrine disputeThe Missionaries of Saint John the Baptist argues that the Kentucky Supreme Court's ruling conflicts with earlier decisions by the US Supreme Court and rulings from other appellate courts. Its lawyers have presented the disagreement between courts as a reason for the nation's highest court to intervene. In its petition, the organisation contends that the legal conflict is longstanding and has been recognised across the lower courts. The outcome could clarify how federal religious land-use protections apply when a religious institution seeks to build on property that is not zoned for that purpose.The neighbourhood family has opposed the appeal, arguing that the case does not warrant intervention by the Supreme Court. Its position is that the dispute concerns a local zoning decision and that the church group has not established why the proposed shrine must be built on the residential property.Supreme Court review brings a local dispute to WashingtonThe Supreme Court's decision to hear the case, announced on October 1, 2026, means the justices will examine the legal questions raised by the competing arguments. The court is expected to hear oral arguments in the coming months, although its decision will determine how the dispute proceeds from there. The case adds to a series of matters before the court involving the relationship between religious rights and government authority. Here, the immediate question concerns a specific piece of land in a Kentucky suburb, but the legal arguments reach beyond the proposed shrine itself.At stake is how federal protections should be applied when religious organisations and local authorities disagree over the use of property. The justices will consider the church group's claim that the state court misapplied federal law alongside the neighbours' argument that ordinary zoning restrictions should stand. For now, the shrine remains the subject of a legal dispute rather than an approved development. The Supreme Court's review will address the legal basis for the church group's challenge, with the eventual ruling expected to shape the next stage of the case.You use AI every day. articles.title: Netanyahu fights for political future as Israel heads to polls with Iran threat looming
articles.summary: Israel heads into a high-stakes election with Benjamin Netanyahu's political future and legacy on the line as voters weigh his security record and the continuing Iran threat.
articles.body: Ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 national vote, President Donald Trump issued a sweeping endorsement of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s re-election bid, calling him a "great warrior," an "even greater partner for peace" and an ally in the confrontation with Iran. The backing could give Israel’s longest-serving prime minister a boost ahead of the country’s first national vote since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, massacre. The election is widely viewed in Israel as a referendum on whether to grant Netanyahu another term to pursue his war objectives, including disarming Hamas and Hezbollah and countering the nuclear threat from the Islamic Republic. In response, Netanyahu thanked Trump for his "extraordinary endorsement." "Together we will never let Iran’s regime get nuclear weapons," he said. TRUMP SAYS NETANYAHU NEEDS TO BE RE-ELECTED, OR ELSE US WILL HAVE TO 'FINISH THE JOB’ AGAINST IRAN ALONE Addressing the endorsement, Doron Spielman, international spokesman for the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office, told Fox News Digital that no personal or professional bond in the history of U.S.-Israel relations compares with the current partnership. "Israel and the U.S. have stood together as the two countries bearing the torch for the West, and that is a direct result of the incredible relationship between President Trump and Netanyahu," he said. He reiterated Netanyahu’s long-standing foreign-policy priority and central campaign promise: ensuring that Iran does not acquire atomic bombs under his watch. "Israel prefers to do this with the U.S., which has been our greatest ally and friend, and who has already entered the front with us twice. But already at the time of Operation Rising Lion, Israel showed that it was willing to act alone. Israel acted for over a week before the U.S. joined," he said, in reference to the June 2025 military mission against Iran. Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, with roughly 20 years in office, Netanyahu began his diplomatic career in 1982 as deputy chief of mission at Israel’s embassy in Washington, D.C. He served as Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations from 1984 to 1988 before entering politics with Likud. He became the party’s chairman in 1993 and was first elected premier in 1996. After losing the 1999 election, Netanyahu returned to government in 2002 as foreign minister and later served as finance minister. He returned to the premiership in 2009, serving until 2021 and again from late 2022. He is widely credited with liberalizing Israel’s economy and helping transform the country into a global high-tech hub. FORMER ISRAELI ARMY CHIEF GADI EISENKOT EMERGES AS NETANYAHU’S LEADING ELECTION CHALLENGER Netanyahu’s current political allies include Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit, Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism-Zehut, and the ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism. The newcomer Amcha Yisrael, led by Ofer Winter, could also join the bloc, although Winter is currently feuding with Likud over concerns that his party, which is hovering near the electoral threshold, could split the right-wing vote and potentially "waste" tens of thousands of ballots. According to most Hebrew-language media polls, neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot currently has a clear path to securing the 61 Knesset seats needed to form a government. If no candidate can assemble a governing coalition, Israel could head to another election, repeating the cycle of political instability that saw the country hold four national votes between April 2019 and March 2021. Dan Diker, president of the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs, told Fox News Digital that any incoming government will face the same formidable security challenges as the current one, with few prospects for quick victories. "The major challenge in this election will be what Netanyahu discussed in terms of adjusting the national security concept to prioritize prevention. That means taking very serious, assertive and aggressive military counterterrorism and nonmilitary actions against our enemies," Diker said. The Israeli left, center and even far-right believe Netanyahu has failed to meet the expectations associated with his image as "Mr. Security," according to professor Tamar Hermann, a senior researcher at the Israel Democracy Institute. ISRAEL DRILLS FOR SURPRISE ATTACK WITH MASSIVE MILITARY EXERCISE AS EXPERT INVOKES 1973 WAR "He promised to topple the Iranian regime, he promised to dismantle Hamas, he promised to crush Hezbollah. None of it was achieved," Hermann told Fox News Digital. "He gave a green light to not punishing vigilantes in the settlements who act against Palestinians. He also gave too much to the ultra-Orthodox parties, giving up on the idea of universal conscription." Hermann said that Netanyahu’s current term has been his least successful, beginning with the judicial reform push, which triggered mass protests in 2023, and followed by the Palestinian terror attacks on Oct. 7. articles.title: Pope's South American trip to go ahead following lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: The Pope underwent surgery in to remove a tumour on the lower part of his right lung and is gradually resuming his duties.
articles.body:
The Vatican has confirmed that Pope Leo will go on his South American tour as planned, following his surgery for lung cancer.

He was diagnosed with lung cancer and underwent successful surgery in Rome on 13 October to remove a tumour on the lower part of his right lung.

The 71-year-old is scheduled to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on 6-17 November, the Vatican said, adding that the he was looking forward to it "with great joy and enthusiasm".

The Pope will follow the same programme as planned, visiting 10 cities on the tour.

"I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I've experienced so many moments of my life," Pope Leo said.

The Pope's trip will begin in Uruguay on 8 November, where he will visit the capital Montevideo, as well as other key cities.

He will then travel to Argentina from November 11-17, visiting a number of places including the capital Buenos Aires.

After that he will spend six days in Peru, where roughly 76% of the population are Catholic, and will include stops in Lima, Chiclayo, Cuzco and Pucallpa.

Peru's Cardinal Castillo, the Archbishop of Lima, has said the trip would involve young people, women who help run community kitchens and members of the country's indigenous communities, according to Vatican News.

The archbishop highlighted the Pope's close ties with the people of Chiclayo, where he lived for several years. The Pope has Peruvian citizenship.

He joined the Augustinian mission in Chulucanas, in the Peruvian department of Piura, and the following year, joined the mission in the city of Trujillo.

For almost three decades, he worked between the US and Peru.

Leo announced the news of his lung operation himself to the world on 11 October during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.

He reassured pilgrims that the growth was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage" but that his doctors had advised him to have it removed.

The surgery lasted for 90 minutes, and he was discharged from Rome's Gemelli hospital on 17 October.

The Pope's surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said he was in an "absolutely satisfactory clinical condition", and said there were "no clinical reasons" why the trip should not go ahead.

Tests showed the cancer was "localised".

Since his operation, the pope has been resting and gradually resuming his work. He has been "adjusting his daily schedule in consultation with his doctors to prioritise his recovery while continuing to fulfill the responsibilities of his ministry," the Vatican said.

Leo was "deeply grateful for the prayers and affection he has received from throughout the world," the Vatican said.

The Vatican said Friday that Leo would cancel a planned trip to Assisi on October 27th, on the recommendation of his doctors.

articles.title: California’s Panamint City had 2,000 residents at its silver boom’s peak in 1874; a flash flood destroyed most of the town two years later
articles.summary: Panamint City in California’s Panamint Mountains had a population of 2,000 at the height of its silver mining boom in 1874.
articles.body: Panamint City in California’s Panamint Mountains had a population of 2,000 at the height of its silver mining boom in 1874. The settlement began when outlaws hiding from the law discovered silver in Surprise Canyon and gave up their life of crime. According to the National Park Service (NPS), the boom was over by the fall of 1875, and a flash flood in 1876 destroyed most of the settlement, leaving only remnants of its former life. The ruins of old Panamint City were added to the park in October 1994. Its old smelter chimney remained as the most prominent reminder of the town that once drew 2,000 people to the mountains.Panamint City grew after outlaws discovered silver in Surprise CanyonPanamint City began with a silver discovery in Surprise Canyon in the Panamint Mountains. Its founders were outlaws who had taken refuge in the mountains while hiding from the law. After finding silver, they gave up their life of crime and established the mining settlement. The discovery attracted people to the area, and the town grew rapidly.By 1874, Panamint City had reached the height of its boom, with a population of 2,000 citizens. The settlement developed a reputation for its rough character and was described as the toughest, rawest place to have passed for a civilised town. The boom did not last long, and by the fall of 1875, the boom was over, bringing Panamint City’s rapid growth to an end.A flash flood destroyed most of Panamint City after its boom had endedBy 1876, a flash flood had destroyed most of Panamint City, which had reached a population of 2,000 at the height of its mining boom in 1874. As reported by NPS, the disaster left few prominent remains of the former settlement. The chimney of the old smelter is the most recognisable reminder of the town’s mining past.In October 1994, the ruins of old Panamint City were added to Death Valley National Park. The surviving chimney and other remains preserve the history of a settlement that grew rapidly after silver was discovered in the remote Panamint Mountains before a natural disaster destroyed much of it.How did mining discoveries lead to the rise of Death Valley’s ghost townsPanamint City was not the only settlement in the Death Valley area to rise and fall with mining activity. Ballarat emerged in 1897 after gold strikes in the Panamint Mountains and had 400 residents in 1898. Greenwater developed around a copper strike in 1905 and grew to a population of 2,000. However, mining collapsed by 1909 without ever showing a profit, and residents left for other areas.Harrisburg grew after a gold strike in 1905 and became a tent city with 300 residents. Skidoo was founded in 1906 after two prospectors discovered gold and eventually reached a population of 700. Like Panamint City, these settlements experienced periods of growth linked to mineral discoveries, although the remains of each town differ.Old smelter, bank building and mines preserve the region’s pastThe former mining settlements around Death Valley contain different traces of their past. Ballarat, which is privately owned, has the ruins of several adobe buildings. Leadfield, heavily mined in 1926, retains wooden and tin building remains, a dugout and cement foundations of a mill, along with mines, tunnels and prospect holes.Rhyolite, the largest town in the Death Valley area, had between 5,000 and 10,000 residents during its heyday from 1905 to 1911. articles.title: Heavenly Creatures killer Pauline Parker dies in Orkney, aged 88
articles.summary: The death of the convicted murderer in Orkney at the age of 88 brings to an end a 70-year story that inspired an acclaimed film.
articles.body:
To her neighbours and friends, Hilary Nathan was a quiet, religious woman who ran a riding stable in the small Orcadian island of Burray.

But her death in an island care home last week at the age of 88 closes a chapter on an extraordinary life that began 70 years ago on the other side of the world with a sensational murder trial.

As a 16-year-old and under her birth name of Pauline Parker, she was convicted alongside her schoolfriend Juliet Hulme of the murder of her mother Honora Parker.

The case shocked New Zealand – and the rest of the world.

The court heard the girls had become inseparable at Christchurch Girls' High School. Fearing that they'd be separated following the divorce of Juliet's parents and a planned move to South Africa, they plotted to kill Mrs Parker, who they believed stood in their way.

They lured her to a park and bludgeoned her to death with a brick inside a stocking.

By the time filmmaker Sir Peter Jackson was born in 1961, both girls had served five years in prison, been released, given new identities, and left New Zealand for good.

"It was known for its tabloid sensational aspect. I know a lot of English tabloids flew to England to cover the case of the 'evil schoolgirl killers'," he told the BBC's Late Show in 1995.

"Repeating that stuff would have been easy, but that's not what we wanted to do. We wanted to understand more about Pauline Parker and Juliet Hulme, and what made them become friends."

His film Heavenly Creatures starred Kate Winslet as Hulme and Melanie Lynskey as Parker. It showed how their intense friendship spilled over into a strange shared fantasy life which culminated in the brutal murder.

The defence argued insanity, but both girls were found guilty of murder and only avoided the death penalty because of their age.

In 1960, having served five years in separate prisons, they were given new identities and moved away from New Zealand.

The court ordered that they should never meet again, and yet they lived part of their lives about 80 miles (129km) apart.

When the film came out in 1995, Juliet was living in Portmahomack in Rosshire, where she'd become a crime writer living under her new name, Anne Perry.

She told the Late Show that she didn't plan to see the film.

"It would be too harrowing," she said. "What was close to the truth would be distressing and what was far from the truth would be even more distressing."

"It's a bit like being stripped naked in the High Street for everyone to come and look and pick and poke. I'd rather put my clothes on and go back home, thank you."

During filming, Kate Winslet said she had no idea where the two women were, and after Anne Perry's identity was revealed, the actress expressed the hope that Pauline Parker would be able to retain her anonymity.

"These are two women who, for the last 40 years, have had to overcome so much in order to get on with their lives and just survive," she said.

But in 2011, Parker was found by lawyer and true-crime author Peter Graham, who had written a book about the case called So Brilliantly Clever, its title taken from her diary, which was used as evidence in court.

She, like Juliet, had come to the UK, where she had settled in a small village in rural Kent and opened a riding school. By 2011, and now known as Hilary Nathan, she had moved to Orkney, running another stable.

For both women, religion and small tight-knit communities provided a haven. According to an interview her sister gave to the New Zealand Women's Weekly, Nathan was a devout Catholic who led a reclusive life.

Perry was a Mormon, enjoying the support of her own community when reporters began to arrive after Heavenly Creatures was released.

She said: "The media descended on Portmahomack. I was horrified, especially since my mother lived in the village. It's not just the people the film is about, it's all the people around them. I felt it might ruin my family."

Although her books were hugely successful in America, she never really found the fame she merited here in the UK, partly because of her reticence to do any promotion.

Prime Suspect creator Lynda La Plante expressed interest in a TV version of Perry's books, but the author vetoed the plan for the same reason.

In 2001, I visited Perry in Portmahomack for a rare interview for Newsnight Scotland. At that stage, she was a glamorous 66-year-old author, with a back catalogue which had sold 15 million copies around the world.

"I think after 51 years, you can let it go," she told me. "It's not who I am now. It's not who I have been for decades."

We didn't talk about the murder directly, but you don't have to look far in her books for insight into what happened and how her life had turned out. Her detective, the Victorian policeman William Monk, suffers from amnesia, and sometimes wonders exactly who he is.

"Monk sees himself as just himself but because of his memory loss, he has to deal with the fact that he may be someone else. That comes from my own sense that other people view me as a monster," she admitted.

"Of course it affects what I write. I have far more compassion and understanding for people who do wrong things than I'd ever have if I hadn't been in that position.

"The questions of right and wrong and compassion and forgiveness concern me in a way they wouldn't have, had I not had the life I had."

Anne Perry died in Los Angeles in 2023 at the age of 88.

Hilary Nathan's death last week at the same age brings their strange story to a close.

How they reinvented themselves out of the world's harshest headlines, and found redemption in the smallest of Scottish communities.

"I would say if you had something which harrowed you, or caused you to feel shame, you should never give up," Anne told me.

"There's more forgiveness, understanding and help out there than you might think."

articles.title: Flood warning lingers in Four Corners as inundated towns face sewage-tainted waters
articles.summary: Parts of the Southwest's Four Corners region remained under a flood warning Monday as some saturated neighborhoods began cleaning up, assessing damage and watching out for water that could be contaminated with sewage.
articles.body: Parts of the Southwest's Four Corners region remained under a flood warning Monday as some saturated neighborhoods began cleaning up, assessing damage and watching out for water that could be contaminated with chemicals and raw sewage. Flooding caused by excessive rainfall happened Monday along the San Juan River in parts of the Four Corners region, the meeting point of Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico. The area has experienced unusually heavy rain since Wednesday that caused rivers to surge, flooding homes and forcing water rescues. Storms led to a tornado that touched down in Santa Fe, New Mexico, on Saturday night. One flooding-related death was reported in Santa Fe on Saturday during a water rescue of a family that had attempted to cross a flooded arroyo in their vehicle, the county sheriff's office said. A father and child were able to get onto land, but a female passenger was swept away by the current and was found dead a mile away, the office said. Rising river has led to evacuations in Utah and Colorado By Monday morning, the San Juan River was 1 1/2 feet above the flood stage of 23 feet, the National Weather Service said. It was expected to crest to 31 feet later Monday, then fall below flood stage by Tuesday morning. This compares to Sept. 10, 1927, when the river crested at 32 feet, the weather service said. Some residents in one community along the river, Bluff, Utah, were evacuated over the weekend but were allowed to return early Monday. Returning residents and businesses should use caution as several properties were still flooded, county officials said. “Stay out of the San Juan River,” the weather service said. “Water levels remain elevated, and possible sewage contamination poses additional health risks.” Farmington area deals with evacuations and power outage In the Farmington area of New Mexico, local officials said swollen rivers were receding, but that many people remained evacuated and hundreds were without power. San Juan County, New Mexico, did not have official figures on the number of homes damaged or how many people were evacuated, spokesperson Devin Neeley told The Associated Press. “It’s a pretty active disaster zone,” he said. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham and Major General Miguel Aguilar of the New Mexico National Guard planned to visit the county Monday to survey damage and meet with affected residents. Floodwaters could be contaminated with chemicals and raw sewage Officials in the hard-hit counties urged patience and caution. Water could be contaminated with chemicals and raw sewage, and gas and propane lines could be broken, among other hazards. “The public is anxious to get back in,” San Juan County Fire & Rescue Chief David Vega acknowledged at a news conference Sunday. “But I want the public to know there are still hazards out there.” Undersheriff Cory Tanner said officials were going from house to house to check for hazards — a process that could take days to complete. Zach and Abigail Flatt started putting together go-bags after receiving evacuation orders on their phones Thursday evening. Their home in Bloomfield, New Mexico, sits on the San Juan River. “In 30 or 40 minutes it had jumped about 4 feet,” Zach recalled Sunday. “After I saw that big jump, and how close it was to going over the banks, I said we've got to get out.” By the time the family was loaded into the car, water was coming up over the tires. They found a hotel room with their two children, ages 2 and 4, and watched via webcams as at least 18 inches of water inundated their property, washing away 22 of their 24 chickens. “We watched stuff just float away, off the porch into the front yard,” Zach said. Authorities are assessing damage in the Navajo Nation and in a Colorado county In the Shiprock, New Mexico, area of the Navajo Nation, wastewater facilities and water holding ponds were damaged by flooding, causing sewage releases into the San Juan River, according to Navajo Tribal Utility Authority Shiprock District Manager Wilfred Franklin Jr. New Mexico's congressional delegation on Sunday urged President Donald Trump to declare an emergency for the state to release federal assistance funding. In Colorado, teams created maps of some counties to help identify affected roads, road closures, impacted areas and evacuation zones. The flooding is just the latest from two months of on-and-off heavy rain in the region caused by tropical moisture coming ashore from the Pacific. After months of drought, other recent deadly flooding struck the Grand Canyon and other areas of New Mexico. Forecasters said El Niño, the natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific, was likely to blame for the latest storm's unusually heavy rainfall.

articles.title: Will the public change its mind about Meghan?
articles.summary: This complicated - and developing - story could prove to be a turning point for Meghan.
articles.body:
The allegations of sexual abuse against Thomas Markle have put his daughter Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, under an uncomfortable spotlight.

She has been dealing with this potential news time-bomb out of sight for seven years, while appearing to share so much about her life in TV series and interviews.

Thomas Markle has strongly rejected the claims as "lies" which are being used to destroy his reputation.

But could this complicated story prove to be a turning point for Meghan, who has had a complicated and often hostile relationship with the UK public?

What has emerged so far means re-thinking some of the criticism she's faced.

Meghan, who recently moved back to the UK with Prince Harry and their children, has frequently been accused of cutting off those once close to her.

Her treatment of her father was seen as a prime example.

"She ditched her family, ditched her dad, ditched most of her old friends, split Harry from William," wrote one commentator in 2020.

"Get on a plane and go see the poor man before it's too late," she was told on social media about her father.

All of that might need to be viewed in a different and more sympathetic light.

By 2019, Meghan had received disturbing allegations about Thomas Markle, in a letter from her father's first wife, Roslyn Loveless.

She says it is why she kept her distance and also why she didn't bring her children to him, including when she moved to the United States with her family.

That letter was shared with Meghan by the police, at a time when she was classified as a working royal. It's not clear who else knew about the letter, including Palace officials, but it must have been a sensitive matter for her.

And according to the Sussexes' spokesman, Meghan believed an investigation into the allegations was going ahead, presumably at a time when she was on official trips and having to put on a brave face.

There was also criticism levelled at Meghan in December 2025 when her father was in hospital in the Philippines, undergoing the amputation of his leg.

"I don't want to die estranged from Meghan. I want to meet my grandkids. It might be nice to meet her husband too," Markle told the Mail on Sunday at the time.

There was a media storm about whether Meghan was going to reach out to her father, culminating in a letter being delivered from her to her father, which at the time was assumed to be well-wishes.

But that whole episode now looks different with the benefit of hindsight. That letter was a much more fraught affair. It revealed that Meghan knew about the allegations against her father.

We now understand that Meghan was telling him he would never see his grandchildren.

Thomas Markle has strongly denied all the allegations against him, saying they are "sick lies" which are trying to destroy his reputation.

His daughter Samantha Markle has also rejected the claims, saying the stories are "fake news" and "clickbait".

"There will be no legal action against my dad with no evidence in so many flimsy stories and my dad never had access to any such content and was in the hospital most of the time that he was there," she wrote on X on Sunday.

Samantha also challenges the credibility of the letter written by her mother, Roslyn Loveless, which was shared with Meghan in 2019 and contained details of allegations of sexual abuse against Thomas Markle.

When you look through photos of Meghan at events over the last seven years, you wonder what was going on behind the familiar smile.

Those years have seen Netflix films, a tell-all memoir by Prince Harry, cookery series, podcasts and TV interviews. But a hidden narrative has been running in the background.

Meghan's supporters have pointed to other factors in how she has been treated, with racism and sexism part of that toxic mix.

But maybe there was also a sense of not knowing the authentic person behind the polished Brand Meghan.

On Instagram, she has curated her life to look idyllic, but perhaps she'll get a more generous hearing now that her back story is as messy and imperfect as everyone else's.

It could still be an uphill struggle to become more popular, beyond her own vocal, core group of supporters.

A survey from YouGov earlier this month found 22% of people had a positive view of Meghan, compared with 49% who dislike her.

That suggests there is still some way to go before Meghan fully wins the trust of the public. Fascination, yes. But affection, not always.

For the British public, Californian Meghan hasn't always translated well.

But perhaps this complex, still developing story - and the light it sheds on previous years - might mean there's a more rounded view of her in the future.

articles.title: OBC candidate scores higher than general aspirant, but didn’t make the cut
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An overage OBC candidate from Tripura became eligible to take the test for recruitment of constables for CAPFs, NIA, Secretariat Security Force
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An overage OBC candidate from Tripura became eligible to take the test for recruitment of constables for CAPFs, NIA, Secretariat Security Force and rifleman in Assam Rifles after taking age-relaxation benefit available for reserved category candidates but was not selected despite securing higher marks than a selected general category candidate.The cut-off mark for OBC candidates was 60, which was higher than that for general category candidates, which the Centre said was because of the limited number of vacancies available in the OBC category. Moreover, once an OBC candidate availed age-relaxation benefit to become eligible, he could not seek migration from reserved category to general category, it said.This resulted in OBC candidate Jayant Debnath, despite securing 55.1 marks in the 2018 recruitment test, not being selected, while general category candidate Sagar Debnath got selected with 46.26 marks.The single-judge bench and the division bench of Tripura HC, concurrently, ruled that Jayant needed to be considered for selection as constable.Appealing against the HC judgements, additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati Monday told an SC bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that recruitment rules clearly specified that once a candidate availed age relaxation on the ground that he belonged to a reserved category, he or she would not be permitted to migrate from reserved category to general category.The bench agreed to examine the correctness of the HC judgement, which had said there was no legal principle prohibiting candidates belonging to reserved categories from claiming unreserved vacancies merely because they had availed benefits applicable to reserved categories.The Centre said, “The present case concerns a candidate who admittedly availed age relaxation exclusively available to OBC candidates and thereby became eligible to participate in the recruitment process only under the reserved category.” It stressed that in such cases, migration from reserved to general category was expressly prohibited by the recruitment rules.“The impugned judgement would have far-reaching consequences for recruitments conducted by SSC and other recruiting agencies throughout the country. It would enable candidates who have availed reservation-specific concessions to seek migration to unreserved vacancies contrary to recruitment rules, thereby unsettling concluded selections, disturbing category-wise merit determination, prejudicing the rights of unreserved candidates, and generating widespread administrative uncertainty in public recruitment.”Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Jordan attacks militants in Syria tied to last week’s church attack, state media says
articles.summary: AMMAN, Jordan — The Jordanian air force carried out strikes against groups in Syria in retaliation for Friday’s attack on a Greek Orthodox Church in Karak that killed nine people, Jordanian state media reported Monday.
articles.body: AMMAN, Jordan — The Jordanian air force carried out strikes against groups in Syria in retaliation for Friday’s attack on a Greek Orthodox Church in Karak that killed nine people, Jordanian state media reported Monday. It said the operation “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles.” It did not specify who the groups were or the precise location of the strikes. Syrian state TV said there were reports of civilian casualties following Jordanian airstrikes south of the village of al-Masmiyah in the southern province of Daraa. Earlier Monday, Jordanian authorities arrested three men for last week’s attack, which also wounded more than two dozen people. The arrests followed a dawn shootout, and all three men were wounded, officials said. The attack struck the Greek Orthodox Church during a funeral in Karak, about 90 kilometers (55 miles) south of the capital, Amman, on Friday. Karak is home to a minority Christian population. The attack shocked the nation, and Jordan declared three days of mourning for the victims. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack; the attackers’ motive remained unknown. Later Monday, the Public Security Directorate identified the three arrested men as brothers Hazzah Zaidan Mohammad and Mishal Zaidan Mohammad, and their brother-in-law Ahmad Sami Hussein. All three are Jordanian; they were taken into custody in Karak, south of Amman. The agency’s chief described the gunmen as “takfiri,” a term used for Sunni militants, but said they were not tied to any organized group. “They only represent themselves,” Maj. Gen. Obaidallah Abd Rabbo Al-Maayta told a news conference. He also said a large cache of munitions was found in the abandoned house where Jordanian forces apprehended the men. Jordan’s Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya said the attack by the three was the result of “a terroristic, extremist way of thinking.” “If this way of thinking is not resolved, we will see incidents like this again,” he told reporters. Jordan’s King Abdullah II had ordered authorities to respond with “an iron fist” against what he called the outlaws of Islam and anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people. “We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he said in a statement on Monday. Relatives of the victims said the arrests brought them some relief. “Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief — and the grief of the Jordanian people — not just for us, the families of the martyrs,” Khaled al-Borqan, himself a survivor of the attack and a relative of three of the people killed, told Al-Mamlaka. “Despite the sadness and pain, the news brought us joy,” Fares Halaseh, an uncle of one of the victims and a survivor of the attack, told the TV station. But the pain remains, he added. “We will not forget this agony for years to come.”
